Terminull Brigade takes the familiar structure of a cooperative third-person shooter and gives it a more unpredictable identity through hero abilities, roguelike upgrades, loot progression, and increasingly intense PvE encounters. Developed by Pew Pew Games and published by Level Infinite, it is built around repeated combat runs through futuristic virtual environments. The emphasis is less on following a rigid sequence of missions and more on entering battles, strengthening a chosen character, experimenting with upgrades, defeating bosses, and discovering how powerful a particular build can become before a run concludes.

The shooting provides a satisfying foundation because combat encourages movement and aggressive positioning instead of prolonged reliance on cover. Firearms remain important, but character-specific abilities prevent every encounter from becoming a simple exercise in aiming and damage output. Different heroes can approach situations in noticeably different ways, giving players reasons to experiment rather than permanently settling on the first character they understand. Mobility, special attacks, weapons, and enemy pressure combine to create battles that frequently become hectic, especially when several players unleash abilities simultaneously.

Its roguelike mechanics are responsible for much of the replayability. Progression during a run can transform an ordinary starting configuration into a dramatically stronger build as upgrades begin interacting with one another. Choosing enhancements becomes part of the strategy because the most effective option is not necessarily the one providing the largest immediate improvement. Building around particular abilities or complementary effects can eventually produce extremely powerful combinations. This gradual escalation provides a strong sense of momentum and makes successful runs feel different from unsuccessful ones.

Cooperative play strengthens the concept further. Although solo play provides a convenient way to learn the mechanics and test heroes, fighting with teammates allows character abilities to complement one another. Coordinated groups can manage enemy crowds, concentrate damage on priority targets, and respond more effectively when encounters become overwhelming. Boss battles are particularly suitable for this structure because they force players to combine movement, offensive timing, survivability, and whatever upgrades they have collected. These confrontations provide some of the clearest tests of whether a build has developed effectively.

The visual direction supports the gameplay with a colorful technological aesthetic centered on simulated worlds and digital environments. The virtual setting gives the designers freedom to introduce unusual locations, enemies, effects, and character designs without needing to remain grounded in realism. Combat can look impressive once numerous abilities and projectiles fill the screen, although this also creates occasional readability problems. During especially crowded fights, distinguishing enemy attacks from friendly effects can become difficult, making the spectacle both an advantage and a potential distraction.

Narrative elements involving Aion, the virtual rebellion, and the mysteries surrounding the digital world give the repeated battles some context, but storytelling is not the primary attraction. The plot serves mainly as motivation for moving deeper into the experience rather than replacing the combat loop as its central focus. Players primarily interested in extensive dialogue, cinematic storytelling, or a traditional linear campaign may consequently find the narrative relatively secondary. Those who prefer gameplay-driven progression are more likely to appreciate the balance.

Repetition remains one of the biggest potential weaknesses. Roguelike progression naturally requires players to revisit the fundamental combat cycle, and enjoyment depends on whether experimenting with different heroes and upgrade combinations provides enough variation. Early sessions can feel exciting because new mechanics and combinations appear frequently, while longer-term play places greater pressure on encounter variety and progression incentives. Players who enjoy optimizing builds can potentially spend considerable time refining strategies, but those who want constantly changing objectives may become fatigued sooner.

The free-to-play framework introduces additional considerations beyond gameplay. In-game purchases are part of the overall structure, and a Level Infinite Pass is required and can be linked to a Steam account. The game also employs Anti-Cheat Expert with kernel-level functionality. These elements will not necessarily affect someone focused exclusively on cooperative combat, but they are relevant for players who dislike additional account requirements or prefer avoiding kernel-level anti-cheat solutions.

Steam Deck compatibility is another significant limitation. The game should not currently be regarded as a dependable Steam Deck title, particularly because SteamOS support and anti-cheat compatibility can present obstacles. Even though its run-based gameplay would theoretically work well in a portable format, anyone purchasing or installing it specifically for Valve's handheld should verify the latest compatibility status rather than expecting seamless operation. For the moment, a conventional Windows PC remains the safer platform for experiencing it as intended.

Ultimately, the game works best when its shooting, hero abilities, randomized progression, and cooperative systems reinforce each other. Creating increasingly powerful builds while fighting through escalating enemy encounters can be highly satisfying, and the virtual science-fiction setting gives those battles an energetic personality. Its weaknesses lie primarily in repetition, live-service considerations, account and anti-cheat requirements, and uncertain handheld suitability. Players who enjoy PvE hero shooters combined with roguelike progression will find a worthwhile action experience here, while those seeking a tightly structured narrative campaign may find its repeated-run philosophy less compelling.

Rating: 7/10
